entries.f904ea0b01066a810fcb9b30ca555b657852ca3c: <div sID="gen3270" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="31" osisID="Num.31" sID="Num.31"/> <div eID="gen3270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3271" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3272" type="x-p"/> This chapter belongs to "the book of the wars of the Lord," in which it is probable it was inserted. It is the history of a holy war, a war with Midian. Here is, I. A divine command for the war, <reference osisRef="Num.31.1-Num.31.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The undertaking of the war, <reference osisRef="Num.31.3-Num.31.6">ver. 3-6</reference>. III. The glorious success of it, <reference osisRef="Num.31.7-Num.31.12">ver. 7-12</reference>. IV. Their triumphant return from the war. 1. The respect Moses paid to the soldiers, <reference osisRef="Num.31.13">ver. 13</reference>. 2. The rebuke he gave them for sparing the women, <reference osisRef="Num.31.14-Num.31.18">ver. 14-18</reference>. 3. The directions he gave them for the purifying of themselves and their effects, <reference osisRef="Num.31.19-Num.31.24">ver. 19-24</reference>. 4. The distribution of the spoil they had taken, one half to the soldiers, the other to the congregation, and a tribute to the Lord out of each, <reference osisRef="Num.31.25-Num.31.47">ver. 25-47</reference>. 5. The free-will offering of the officers, <reference osisRef="Num.31.48-Num.31.54">ver. 48</reference>, &c.
entries.a880d4d39e96daacf3f9a9464c1c54e6590fabed: <div eID="gen3272" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3271" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Slaughter of the Midianites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3273" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Avenge the children of Israel of the Midianites: afterward shalt thou be gathered unto thy people. 3 And Moses spake unto the people, saying, Arm some of yourselves unto the war, and let them go against the Midianites, and avenge the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of Midian. 4 Of every tribe a thousand, throughout all the tribes of Israel, shall ye send to the war. <hi type="super">5</hi> So there were delivered out of the thousands of Israel, a thousand of <hi type="italic">every</hi> tribe, twelve thousand armed for war. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Moses sent them to the war, a thousand of <hi type="italic">every</hi> tribe, them and Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, to the war, with the holy instruments, and the trumpets to blow in his hand. <div eID="gen3273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3274" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The Lord of hosts gives orders to Moses to make war upon the Midianites, and his commission no doubt justified this war, though it will not serve to justify the like without such commission. The Midianites were the posterity of Abraham by Keturah, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.2">Gen. xxv. 2</reference>. Some of them settled south of Canaan, among whom Jethro lived, and they retained the worship of the true God; but these were settled east of Canaan, and had fallen into idolatry, neighbours to, and in confederacy with, the Moabites. Their land was not designed to be given to Israel, nor would Israel have meddled with them if they had not made themselves obnoxious to their resentment by sending their bad women among them to draw them to whoredom and idolatry. This was the provocation, this was the quarrel. For this (says God) <hi type="italic">avenge Israel of the Midianites,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.31.2">v. 2</reference>. 1. God would have the Midianites chastised, an inroad made upon that part of their country which lay next to the camp of Israel, and which was probably more concerned in that mischief than the Moabites, who therefore were let alone. God will have us to reckon those our worst enemies that draw us to sin, and to avoid them; and since <hi type="italic">every man is tempted when he is drawn aside of his own lusts,</hi> and these are the Midianites which ensnare us with their wiles, on them we should avenge ourselves, not only make no league with them, but make war upon them by living a life of mortification. God had taken vengeance on his own people for yielding to the Midianites' temptations; now the Midianites, that gave the temptation, must be reckoned with, for <hi type="italic">the deceived and the deceiver are his</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.12.16">Job xii. 16</reference>), both accountable to his tribunal; and, though <hi type="italic">judgment begin at the house of God,</hi> it shall not end there, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1 Pet. iv. 17</reference>. There is a day coming when vengeance will be taken on those that have introduced errors and corruptions into the church, and the devil that deceived men will be <hi type="italic">cast into the lake of fire.</hi> Israel's quarrel with Amalek, that fought against them, was not avenged till long after: but their quarrel with Midian, that debauched them, was speedily avenged, for they were looked upon as much more the dangerous and malicious enemies. 2. God would have it done by Moses, in his life-time, that he who had so deeply resented that injury might have the satisfaction of seeing it avenged. "See this execution done upon the enemies of God and Israel, and <hi type="italic">afterwards thou shalt be gathered to thy people.</hi>" This was the only piece of service of this kind that Moses must further do, and then he has accomplished, as a hireling, his day, and shall have his <hi type="italic">quietus—enter into rest:</hi> hitherto his usefulness must come, and no further; the wars of Canaan must be carried on by another hand. Note, God sometimes removes useful men when we think they can be ill spared; but this ought to satisfy us, that they are never removed till they have done the work which was appointed them. <div eID="gen3274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3275" type="x-p"/> II. Moses gives orders to the people to prepare for this expedition, <reference osisRef="Num.31.3">v. 3</reference>. He would not have the whole body of the camp to stir, but they must <hi type="italic">arm some of themselves to the war,</hi> such as were either most fit or most forward, and <hi type="italic">avenge the Lord of Midian.</hi> God said, <hi type="italic">Avenge Israel;</hi> Moses says, <hi type="italic">Avenge the Lord;</hi> for the interests of God and Israel are united, and the cause of both is one and the same. And if God, in what he does, shows himself jealous for the honour of Israel, surely Israel, in what they do, ought to show themselves jealous for the glory of God. Then only we can justify the avenging of ourselves when it is the vengeance of the Lord that we engage in. Nay, for this reason we are forbidden to avenge ourselves, because God has said, <hi type="italic">Vengeance is mine, I will repay.</hi> <div eID="gen3275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3276" type="x-p"/> III. A detachment is drawn out accordingly for this service, 1000 <hi type="italic">out of every tribe,</hi> 12,000 in all, a small number in comparison with what they could have sent, and it is probable small in comparison with the number of the enemies they were sent against. But God would teach them that it is all one to him <hi type="italic">to save by many or by few,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">1 Sam. xiv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen3276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3277" type="x-p"/> IV. Phinehas the son of Eleazar is sent along with them. It is strange that no mention is made of Joshua in this great action. If he was general of these forces, who do we not find him leading them out? If he tarried at home, why do we not find him meeting them with Moses at their return? It is probable, each tribe having a captain of its own thousand, there was no general, but they proceeded in the order of their march through the wilderness, Judah first, and the rest in their posts, under the command of their respective captains, spoken of <reference osisRef="Num.31.48">v. 48</reference>. But, the war being a holy war, Phinehas was their common head, not to supply the place of a general, but, by the oracle of God, to determine the resolves of their counsels of war, in which the captains of thousands would all acquiesce, and according to which they would act in conjunction. He therefore took with him the holy instruments or vessels, probably the breast-plate of judgment, by which God might he consulted in any emergency. Though he was not yet the high priest, yet he might be delegated <hi type="italic">pro hac vice—for this particular occasion,</hi> to bear the urim and thummim, as <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.6">1 Sam. xxiii. 6</reference>. And there was a particular reason for sending Phinehas to preside in this expedition; he has already signalized himself for his zeal against the Midianites and their cursed arts to ensnare Israel when he slew Cozbi, a daughter of a chief house in Midian, for her impudence in the matter of Peor, <reference osisRef="Num.25.15">ch. xxv. 15</reference>. He that had so well used the sword of justice against a particular criminal was best qualified to guide the sword of war against the whole nation. <hi type="italic">Thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things.</hi>
entries.668f67222c7d27d29b7ee64c1bbb3357ff0e1100: <div eID="gen3277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3278" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And they warred against the Midianites, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses; and they slew all the males. <hi type="super">8</hi> And they slew the kings of Midian, beside the rest of them that were slain; <hi type="italic">namely,</hi> Evi, and Rekem, and Zur, and Hur, and Reba, five kings of Midian: Balaam also the son of Beor they slew with the sword. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the children of Israel took <hi type="italic">all</hi> the women of Midian captives, and their little ones, and took the spoil of all their cattle, and all their flocks, and all their goods. <hi type="super">10</hi> And they burnt all their cities wherein they dwelt, and all their goodly castles, with fire. 11 And they took all the spoil, and all the prey, <hi type="italic">both</hi> of men and of beasts. <hi type="super">12</hi> And they brought the captives, and the prey, and the spoil, unto Moses, and Eleazar the priest, and unto the congregation of the children of Israel, unto the camp at the plains of Moab, which <hi type="italic">are</hi> by Jordan <hi type="italic">near</hi> Jericho. <div eID="gen3278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3279" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The descent which this little army of Israelites made, under the divine commission, conduct, and command, upon the country of Midian. They <hi type="italic">warred against the Midianites.</hi> It is very probable that they first published their manifesto, showing the reasons of the war, and requiring them to give up the ringleaders of the mischief to justice; for such afterwards was the <hi type="italic">law</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.10">Deut. xx. 10</reference>), and such the <hi type="italic">practice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.20.12-Judg.20.13">Judg. xx. 12, 13</reference>. But the Midianites justifying what they had done, and standing by those that had done it, the Israelites attacked them with fire and sword, and all the pious fury with which their zeal for God and their people inspired them. 2. The execution (the military execution) they did in this descent. (1.) <hi type="italic">They slew all the males</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.31.7">v. 7</reference>), that is, all they met with as far as they went; they put them all to the sword, and gave no quarter. But that they did not slay all the males of the nation is certain, for we find the Midianites a powerful and formidable enemy to Israel in the days of Gideon; and they were the Midianites of this country, for they are reckoned with the <hi type="italic">children of the east,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.6.3">Judg. vi. 3</reference>. (2.) They <hi type="italic">slew the kings of Midian</hi> the same that are called <hi type="italic">elders of Midian</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.22.4">ch. xxii. 4</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">dukes of Sihon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.13.21">Josh. xiii. 21</reference>. Five of these princes are here named, one of whom is <hi type="italic">Zur,</hi> probably the same Zur whose daughter Cosbi was, <reference osisRef="Num.25.15">ch. xxv. 15</reference>. (3.) They slew Balaam. Many conjectures there are as to what brought Balaam among the Midianites at this time; it is probable that the Midianites, having intelligence of the march of this army of Israelites against them, hired Balaam to come and assist them with his enchantments, that if he could not prevail to act offensively in their favour, by cursing the armies of Israel, yet he might act defensively, by blessing the country of Midian. Whatever was the occasion of his being there, God's overruling providence brought him thither, and there his just vengeance found him. Had he himself believed what he said of the happy state of Israel, he would not have herded thus with the enemies of Israel; but justly does he die the death of the wicked (though he pretended to desire that of the righteous), and go <hi type="italic">down slain to the pit with the uncircumcised,</hi> who rebelled thus against the convictions of his own conscience. The Midianites' wiles were Balaam's projects, it was therefore just that he should perish with them, <reference osisRef="Hos.4.5">Hos. iv. 5</reference>. Now was <hi type="italic">his</hi> folly made manifest to all men, who foretold the fate of others, but foresaw not his own. (4.) They took all the <hi type="italic">women and children captives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.31.9">v. 9</reference>. (5.) They <hi type="italic">burnt their cities and goodly castles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.31.10">v. 10</reference>), not designing to inhabit them themselves (that country was out of their line), but they thus prevented those who had made their escape from sheltering themselves in their own country and settling there again. Some understand it of their idol-temples; it was fit that they should share in this vengeance. (6.) They plundered the country, and carried off all the cattle and valuable goods, and so returned to the camp of Israel laden with a very rich booty, <reference osisRef="Num.31.9">v. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.11">11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.12">12</reference>. Thus (as when they came out of Egypt) they were enriched with the spoils of their enemies, and furnished with stock for the good land into which God was bringing them.
entries.18528354b5d00482cf963002124e0da74f378d80: <div eID="gen3279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3280" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And Moses, and Eleazar the priest, and all the princes of the congregation, went forth to meet them without the camp. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Moses was wroth with the officers of the host, <hi type="italic">with</hi> the captains over thousands, and captains over hundreds, which came from the battle. <hi type="super">15</hi> And Moses said unto them, Have ye saved all the women alive? <hi type="super">16</hi> Behold, these caused the children of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to commit trespass against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the matter of Peor, and there was a plague among the congregation of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">17</hi> Now therefore kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman that hath known man by lying with him. <hi type="super">18</hi> But all the women children, that have not known a man by lying with him, keep alive for yourselves. <hi type="super">19</hi> And do ye abide without the camp seven days: whosoever hath killed any person, and whosoever hath touched any slain, purify <hi type="italic">both</hi> yourselves and your captives on the third day, and on the seventh day. <hi type="super">20</hi> And purify all <hi type="italic">your</hi> raiment, and all that is made of skins, and all work of goats' <hi type="italic">hair,</hi> and all things made of wood. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Eleazar the priest said unto the men of war which went to the battle, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the ordinance of the law which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses; <hi type="super">22</hi> Only the gold, and the silver, the brass, the iron, the tin, and the lead, 23 Every thing that may abide the fire, ye shall make <hi type="italic">it</hi> go through the fire, and it shall be clean: nevertheless it shall be purified with the water of separation: and all that abideth not the fire ye shall make go through the water. <hi type="super">24</hi> And ye shall wash your clothes on the seventh day, and ye shall be clean, and afterward ye shall come into the camp. <div eID="gen3280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3281" type="x-p"/> We have here the triumphant return of the army of Israel from the war with Midian, and here, <div eID="gen3281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3282" type="x-p"/> I. They were met with great respect, <reference osisRef="Num.31.13">v. 13</reference>. Moses himself, notwithstanding his age and gravity, walked out of the camp to congratulate them on their victory, and to grace the solemnity of their triumphs. Public successes should be publicly acknowledged, to the glory of God, and the encouragement of those that have jeoparded their lives in their country's cause. <div eID="gen3282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3283" type="x-p"/> II. They were severely reproved for saving the women alive. It is very probable that Moses had commanded them to kill the women, at least this was implied in the general order to avenge Israel of the Midianites; the execution having reference to that crime, their drawing them in to the worship of Peor, it was easy to conclude that the women, who were the principal criminals, must not be spared. What! says Moses, <hi type="italic">have you saved the women alive?</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.31.15">v. 15</reference>. He was moved with a holy indignation at the sight of them. <hi type="italic">These were those that caused the children of Israel to commit this trespass;</hi> and therefore, 1. It is just that they should die. The law in case of whoredom was, <hi type="italic">The adulterer and adulteress should surely be put to death.</hi> God had put to death the adulterers of Israel by the plague, and now it was fit that the adulteresses of Midian, especially since they had been the tempters, should be put to death by the sword. 2. "It is dangerous to let them live; they will be still tempting the Israelites to uncleanness, and so your captives will be your conquerors and a second time your destroyers." Severe orders are therefore given that all the grown women should be slain in cold blood, and only the female children spared. <div eID="gen3283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3284" type="x-p"/> III. They were obliged to purify themselves, according to the ceremony of the law, and to abide without the camp seven days, till their purification was accomplished. For, 1. They had imbrued their hands in blood, by which though they had not contracted any moral guilt, the war being just and lawful, yet they were brought under a ceremonial uncleanness, which rendered them unfit to come near the tabernacle till they were purified. Thus God would preserve in their minds a dread and detestation of murder. David must not build the temple because he had been a <hi type="italic">man of war, and had shed blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.3">1 Chron. xxviii. 3</reference>. 2. They could not but have touched dead bodies, by which they were polluted, and that required they should be purified with the water of separation, <reference osisRef="Num.31.19-Num.31.20">v. 19, 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.24">24</reference>. <div eID="gen3284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3285" type="x-p"/> IV. They must likewise purify the spoil they had taken, the captives (<reference osisRef="Num.31.19">v. 19</reference>) and all the goods, <reference osisRef="Num.31.21-Num.31.23">v. 21-23</reference>. What would bear the fire must pass through the fire, and what would not must be washed with water. These things had been use by Midianites, and, having now come into the possession of Israelites, it was fit that they should be sanctified to the service of that holy nation and the honour of their holy God. To us now every thing is sanctified by the word and prayer, if we are sanctified by the Spirit, who is compared both to fire and water. <hi type="italic">To the pure all things are pure.</hi>
entries.2a7393c7eb9a41e8d8655be0bb51d36e0ec8518e: <div eID="gen3285" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Distribution of the Spoil. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3286" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">26</hi> Take the sum of the prey that was taken, <hi type="italic">both</hi> of man and of beast, thou, and Eleazar the priest, and the chief fathers of the congregation: <hi type="super">27</hi> And divide the prey into two parts; between them that took the war upon them, who went out to battle, and between all the congregation: 28 And levy a tribute unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of the men of war which went out to battle: one soul of five hundred, <hi type="italic">both</hi> of the persons, and of the beeves, and of the asses, and of the sheep: <hi type="super">29</hi> Take <hi type="italic">it</hi> of their half, and give it unto Eleazar the priest, <hi type="italic">for</hi> an heave offering of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">30</hi> And of the children of Israel's half, thou shalt take one portion of fifty, of the persons, of the beeves, of the asses, and of the flocks, of all manner of beasts, and give them unto the Levites, which keep the charge of the tabernacle of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">31</hi> And Moses and Eleazar the priest did as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the booty, <hi type="italic">being</hi> the rest of the prey which the men of war had caught, was six hundred thousand and seventy thousand and five thousand sheep, <hi type="super">33</hi> And threescore and twelve thousand beeves, <hi type="super">34</hi> And threescore and one thousand asses, <hi type="super">35</hi> And thirty and two thousand persons in all, of women that had not known man by lying with him. <hi type="super">36</hi> And the half, <hi type="italic">which was</hi> the portion of them that went out to war, was in number three hundred thousand and seven and thirty thousand and five hundred sheep: 37 And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's tribute of the sheep was six hundred and threescore and fifteen. <hi type="super">38</hi> And the beeves <hi type="italic">were</hi> thirty and six thousand; of which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's tribute <hi type="italic">was</hi> threescore and twelve. <hi type="super">39</hi> And the asses <hi type="italic">were</hi> thirty thousand and five hundred; of which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's tribute <hi type="italic">was</hi> threescore and one. <hi type="super">40</hi> And the persons <hi type="italic">were</hi> sixteen thousand; of which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's tribute <hi type="italic">was</hi> thirty and two persons. <hi type="super">41</hi> And Moses gave the tribute, <hi type="italic">which was</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's heave offering, unto Eleazar the priest, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses. <hi type="super">42</hi> And of the children of Israel's half, which Moses divided from the men that warred, <hi type="super">43</hi> (Now the half <hi type="italic">that pertained unto</hi> the congregation was three hundred thousand and thirty thousand <hi type="italic">and</hi> seven thousand and five hundred sheep, 44 And thirty and six thousand beeves, <hi type="super">45</hi> And thirty thousand asses and five hundred, <hi type="super">46</hi> And sixteen thousand persons;) <hi type="super">47</hi> Even of the children of Israel's half, Moses took one portion of fifty, <hi type="italic">both</hi> of man and of beast, and gave them unto the Levites, which kept the charge of the tabernacle of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses. <div eID="gen3286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3287" type="x-p"/> We have here the distribution of the spoil which was taken in this expedition against Midian. God himself directed how it should be distributed, and Moses and Eleazar did according to the directions, and thus unhappy contests among themselves were prevented and the victory was made to turn to the common benefit. It was fit that he who gave them the prey should order the disposal of it. All we have is from God, and therefore must be subject to his will. <div eID="gen3287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3288" type="x-p"/> I. The prey is ordered to be divided into two parts, one for the 12,000 men that undertook the war, and the other for the congregation. The prey that was divided seems to have been only the captives and the cattle; as for the plate, and jewels, and other goods, every man kept what he took, as is intimated, <reference osisRef="Num.31.50-Num.31.53">v. 50-53</reference>. That only was distributed which would be of use for the stocking of that good land into which they were going. Now observe, 1. That the one half of the prey was given to the whole congregation, Moses allotting to each tribe its share, and then leaving it to the heads of the tribes to divide their respective shares among themselves, according to their families. The war was undertaken on the behalf of the whole congregation; they would all have been ready to <hi type="italic">go to the help of the Lord against the mighty,</hi> if they had been so ordered, and they did help, it is likely, by their prayers; and therefore God appoints that those that <hi type="italic">tarried at home should divide the spoil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.12">Ps. lxviii. 12</reference>. David, in his time, made it a <hi type="italic">statute and an ordinance for Israel,</hi> that, as his part is that <hi type="italic">goes down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.24-1Sam.30.25">1 Sam. xxx. 24, 25</reference>. Those that are employed in public trusts must not think to benefit themselves only by their toils and hazards, but must aim at the advantage of the community. 2. That yet the 12,000 that went to the battle had as much for their share as the whole congregation (which were fifty times as many) had for theirs; so that the particular persons of the soldiery had a much better share than any of their brethren that tarried at home: and good reason they should. The greater pains we take, and the greater hazards we run, in the service of God and our generation, the greater will our recompence be at last; for <hi type="italic">God is not unrighteous to forget the work and labour of love.</hi> <div eID="gen3288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3289" type="x-p"/> II. God was to have a tribute out of it, as an acknowledgment of his sovereignty over them in general, and that he was their king to whom <hi type="italic">tribute was due,</hi> and particularly of his interest in this war and the gains of it, he having given them their success; and that the priests, the Lord's receivers, might have something added to the provision made for their maintenance. Note, Whatever we have, God must have his dues out of it. And here (as before) the soldiers are favoured above the rest of the congregation, for out of the people's share God required one in fifty, but out of the soldier's share only one in 500, because the people got theirs easily, without any peril or fatigue. The less opportunity we have of honouring God with our personal services the more it is expected we should honour him with our substance. The tribute out of the soldiers' half was given to the priests (<reference osisRef="Num.31.29">v. 29</reference>), that out of the people's half was given to the Levites, <reference osisRef="Num.31.30">v. 30</reference>. For the priests were taken from among the Levites, as these soldiers from among the people, for special and hazardous service, and their pay was proportioned accordingly.
entries.6936a23416f0a5f4e91421eeb2a4e38b5eabe30d: <div eID="gen3289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3290" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">48</hi> And the officers which <hi type="italic">were</hi> over thousands of the host, the captains of thousands, and captains of hundreds, came near unto Moses: <hi type="super">49</hi> And they said unto Moses, Thy servants have taken the sum of the men of war which <hi type="italic">are</hi> under our charge, and there lacketh not one man of us. <hi type="super">50</hi> We have therefore brought an oblation for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , what every man hath gotten, of jewels of gold, chains, and bracelets, rings, earrings, and tablets, to make an atonement for our souls before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">51</hi> And Moses and Eleazar the priest took the gold of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all wrought jewels. <hi type="super">52</hi> And all the gold of the offering that they offered up to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , of the captains of thousands, and of the captains of hundreds, was sixteen thousand seven hundred and fifty shekels. <hi type="super">53</hi> (<hi type="italic">For</hi> the men of war had taken spoil, every man for himself.) <hi type="super">54</hi> And Moses and Eleazar the priest took the gold of the captains of thousands and of hundreds, and brought it into the tabernacle of the congregation, <hi type="italic">for</hi> a memorial for the children of Israel before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen3290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3291" type="x-p"/> Here is a great example of piety and devotion in the officers of the army, the colonels, that are called <hi type="italic">captains of thousands,</hi> and the inferior officers that were <hi type="italic">captains of hundreds;</hi> they came to Moses as their general and commander-in-chief, and, though he was now going off the stage they very humbly and respectfully addressed themselves to him, calling themselves his <hi type="italic">servants;</hi> the honours they had won did not puff them up, so as to make them forget their duty to him. Observe in their address to them, 1. The pious notice they take of God's wonderful goodness to them in this late expedition, in preserving not only their own lives, but the lives of all the men of war that they had under their charge; so that, upon the review of their muster-roll, it appeared there was not one missing, <reference osisRef="Num.31.49">v. 49</reference>. This was very extraordinary, and perhaps cannot be paralleled in any history. So many thousands of lives jeoparded in the high places of the field, and not one lost, either by the sword of the enemy or by any disease or disaster. This was <hi type="italic">the Lord's doing,</hi> and cannot but be marvellous in the eyes of those that consider how the lives of all men, especially soldiers, are continually in their hands. It is an evidence of the tender feeling which these commanders had for their soldiers, and that their lives were very precious to them, that they looked upon it as a mercy to themselves that none of those under their charge miscarried. <hi type="italic">Of all that were given them they had lost none;</hi> so precious also is the blood of Christ's subjects and soldiers to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.14">Ps. lxxii. 14</reference>. 2. The pious acknowledgment they make for this favour: <hi type="italic">Therefore we have brought an oblation to the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.31.50">v. 50</reference>. The oblation they brought was out of that which <hi type="italic">every man had gotten,</hi> and it was gotten honestly by a divine warrant. Thus every man should lay by <hi type="italic">according as God has prospered him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1 Cor. xvi. 2</reference>. For where God sows plentifully in the gifts of his bounty he expects to reap accordingly in the fruits of our piety and charity. The tabernacle first, and the temple afterwards, were beautified and enriched with the spoils taken from the enemies of Israel; as by David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.11-2Sam.8.12">2 Sam. viii. 11, 12</reference>), and his captains, <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.26-1Chr.26.27">1 Chron. xxvi. 26, 27</reference>. We should never take any thing to ourselves, in war or trade, which we cannot in faith consecrate a part of to God, who <hi type="italic">hates robbery for burnt-offerings;</hi> but, when God has remarkably preserved and prospered us, he expects that we should make some particular return of gratitude to him. As to this oblation, (1.) The captains offered it to <hi type="italic">make an atonement for their souls,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.31.50">v. 50</reference>. Instead of coming to Moses to demand a recompence for the good service they had done in <hi type="italic">avenging the Lord of Midian,</hi> or to set up trophies of their victory for the immortalizing of their own names, they bring an oblation to <hi type="italic">make atonement for their souls,</hi> being conscious to themselves, as the best men must be even in their best services, that they had been defective in their duty, not only in that instance for which they were reproved (<reference osisRef="Num.31.14">v. 14</reference>), but in many others; <hi type="italic">for there is not a just man upon the earth that doeth good and sinneth not.</hi> (2.) Moses accepted it, and laid it up in the tabernacle <hi type="italic">as a memorial for the children of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.31.54">v. 54</reference>), that is, a monument of God's goodness to them, that they might be encouraged to trust in him in their further wars, and a monument of their gratitude to God (sacrifices are said to be memorials), that he, being well pleased with this thankful acknowledgment of favours bestowed, might continue and repeat his mercies to them.  <chapter eID="Num.31"/> <div eID="gen3291" type="x-p"/>

entries.0b5b1d3f65baf88701469b0a410e52a2ee2dac6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1580"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 31</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.31.1-Num.31.54">Nu 31:1-54</reference>. The Midianites Spoiled and Balaam Slain.</title> <div sID="gen2119" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1580"/><hi type="bold">1-2. the Lord spake unto Moses, Avenge the children of Israel of the Midianites--</hi>a semi-nomad people, descended from Abraham and Keturah, occupying a tract of country east and southeast of Moab, which lay on the eastern coast of the Dead Sea. They seem to have been the principal instigators of the infamous scheme of seduction, planned to entrap the Israelites into the double crime of idolatry and licentiousness [Nu 25:<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.17">1-3, 17</reference>, 18] by which, it was hoped, the Lord would withdraw from that people the benefit of His protection and favor. Moreover, the Midianites had rendered themselves particularly obnoxious by entering into a hostile league with the Amorites (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.21">Jos 13:21</reference>). The Moabites were at this time spared in consideration of Lot (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.9">De 2:9</reference>) and because the measure of their iniquities was not yet full. God spoke of avenging "the children of Israel" [Nu 31:2]; Moses spoke of avenging the Lord [Nu 31:3], as dishonor had been done to God and an injury inflicted on His people. The interests were identical. God and His people have the same cause, the same friends, and the same assailants. This, in fact, was a religious war, undertaken by the express command of God against idolaters, who had seduced the Israelites to practise their abominations. <div eID="gen2119" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebedab82bccddeac240e72f8942fc4c62c3de87e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1581"/><div sID="gen2120" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1581"/><hi type="bold">3. Arm some of yourselves--</hi>This order was issued but a short time before the death of Moses. The announcement to him of that approaching event [Nu 31:2] seems to have accelerated, rather than retarded, his warlike preparations. <div eID="gen2120" type="x-p"/>
entries.a47906838dbef1427861fead4d15d8be968be4a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1582"/><div sID="gen2121" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1582"/><hi type="bold">5. there were delivered--</hi>that is, drafted, chosen, an equal amount from each tribe, to prevent the outbreak of mutual jealousy or strife. Considering the numerical force of the enemy, this was a small quota to furnish. But the design was to exercise their faith and animate them to the approaching invasion of Canaan. <div eID="gen2121" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d68ffdf2c1eff7dc86f2bc542035185224a4853: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1583"/><div sID="gen2122" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1583"/><hi type="bold">6. Moses sent ... Eleazar the priest, to the war--</hi>Although it is not expressly mentioned, it is highly probable that Joshua was the general who conducted this war. The presence of the priest, who was always with the army (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.2">De 20:2</reference>), was necessary to preside over the Levites, who accompanied the expedition, and to inflame the courage of the combatants by his sacred services and counsels.<div eID="gen2122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy instruments--</hi>As neither the ark nor the Urim and Thummim were carried to the battlefield till a later period in the history of Israel, the "holy instruments" must mean the "trumpets" (<reference osisRef="Num.10.9">Nu 10:9</reference>). And this view is agreeable to the text, by simply changing "and" into "even," as the Hebrew particle is frequently rendered. <div eID="gen2123" type="x-p"/>
entries.efe230fe2f5fc45651a0e6580d2f11d5f67942bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1584"/><div sID="gen2124" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1584"/><hi type="bold">7. they slew all the males--</hi>This was in accordance with a divine order in all such cases (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.13">De 20:13</reference>). But the destruction appears to have been only partial--limited to those who were in the neighborhood of the Hebrew camp and who had been accomplices in the villainous plot of Baal-peor (<reference osisRef="Num.25.1-Num.25.3">Nu 25:1-3</reference>), while a large portion of the Midianites were absent on their pastoral wanderings or had saved themselves by flight. (Compare <reference osisRef="Judg.6.1">Jud 6:1</reference>). <div eID="gen2124" type="x-p"/>
entries.b914e36621dfbb946afd28b5120c2446318710c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1585"/><div sID="gen2125" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1585"/><hi type="bold">8. the kings of Midian--</hi>so called, because each was possessed of absolute power within his own city or district; called also dukes or princes of Sihon (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.21">Jos 13:21</reference>), having been probably subject to that Amorite ruler, as it is not uncommon in the East to find a number of governors or pachas tributary to one great king.<div eID="gen2125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zur--</hi>father of Cozbi (<reference osisRef="Num.25.15">Nu 25:15</reference>).<div eID="gen2126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Balaam also ... they slew with the sword--</hi>This unprincipled man, on his dismissal from Balak, set out for his home in Mesopotamia (<reference osisRef="Num.24.25">Nu 24:25</reference>). But, either diverging from his way to tamper with the Midianites, he remained among them without proceeding farther, to incite them against Israel and to watch the effects of his wicked counsel; or, learning in his own country that the Israelites had fallen into the snare which he had laid and which he doubted not would lead to their ruin, he had, under the impulse of insatiable greed, returned to demand his reward from the Midianites. He was an object of merited vengeance. In the immense slaughter of the Midianitish people--in the capture of their women, children, and property and in the destruction of all their places of refuge--the severity of a righteous God fell heavily on that base and corrupt race. But, more than all others, Balaam deserved and got the just reward of his deeds. His conduct had been atrociously sinful, considering the knowledge he possessed, and the revelations he had received, of the will of God. For any one in his circumstances to attempt defeating the prophecies he had himself been the organ of uttering, and plotting to deprive the chosen people of the divine favor and protection, was an act of desperate wickedness, which no language can adequately characterize. <div eID="gen2127" type="x-p"/>
entries.df343b14500cd60ef8774da80a79b8eaf0921fa0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1586"/><div sID="gen2128" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1586"/><hi type="bold">13. Moses, and Eleazar the priest, ... went forth to meet them without the camp--</hi>partly as a token of respect and congratulation on their victory, partly to see how they had executed the Lord's commands, and partly to prevent the defilement of the camp by the entrance of warriors stained with blood. <div eID="gen2128" type="x-p"/>
entries.250dfb2a677c669443d7db48940a8fdadc67399d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1587"/><div sID="gen2129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1587"/><hi type="bold">14-18. And Moses was wroth with the officers of the host--</hi>The displeasure of the great leader, though it appears the ebullition of a fierce and sanguinary temper, arose in reality from a pious and enlightened regard to the best interests of Israel. No order had been given for the slaughter of the women, and in ancient war they were commonly reserved for slaves. By their antecedent conduct, however, the Midianitish women had forfeited all claims to mild or merciful treatment; and the sacred character, the avowed object of the war (<reference osisRef="Num.31.2">Nu 31:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.3">3</reference>), made their slaughter necessary without any special order. But why "kill every male among the little ones"? It was designed to be a war of extermination, such as God Himself had ordered against the people of Canaan, whom the Midianites equalled in the enormity of their wickedness. <div eID="gen2129" type="x-p"/>
entries.752567b0dee806be2354130ed1aaa7c036c6d8ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1588"/><div sID="gen2130" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1588"/><hi type="bold">19-24. abide without the camp seven days: whosoever hath killed any person ... purify both yourselves and your captives--</hi>Though the Israelites had taken the field in obedience to the command of God, they had become defiled by contact with the dead. A process of purification was to be undergone, as the law required (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.13">Le 15:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.19.9-Num.19.12">Nu 19:9-12</reference>), and this purifying ceremony was extended to dress, houses, tents, to everything on which a dead body had lain, which had been touched by the blood-stained hands of the Israelitish warriors, or which had been the property of idolaters. This became a standing ordinance in all time coming (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.28">Le 6:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.11.33">11:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.15.12">15:12</reference>). <div eID="gen2130" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e4e43c20c7d8f016205ec78b5c6b212a3657351: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1589"/><div sID="gen2131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1589"/><hi type="bold">25-39. Take the sum of the prey that was taken--</hi>that is, of the captives and cattle, which, having been first lumped together according to ancient usage (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.9">Ex 15:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.5.30">Jud 5:30</reference>), were divided into two equal parts: the one to the people at large, who had sustained a common injury from the Midianites and who were all liable to serve: and the other portion to the combatants, who, having encountered the labors and perils of war, justly received the largest share. From both parts, however, a certain deduction was taken for the sanctuary, as a thank offering to God for preservation and for victory. The soldiers had greatly the advantage in the distribution; for a five-hundredth part only of their half went to the priest, while a fiftieth part of the congregation's half was given to the Levites. <div eID="gen2131" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0a16c3f42bdafc366646a2454e0cd50b85fe4a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1591"/><div sID="gen2133" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1591"/><hi type="bold">48-54. officers ... said ... there lacketh not one man of us--</hi>A victory so signal, and the glory of which was untarnished by the loss of a single Israelitish soldier, was an astonishing miracle. So clearly betokening the direct interposition of Heaven, it might well awaken the liveliest feelings of grateful acknowledgment to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.2">Psa 44:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">3</reference>). The oblation they brought for the Lord "was partly an atonement" or reparation for their error (<reference osisRef="Num.31.14-Num.31.16">Nu 31:14-16</reference>), for it could not possess any expiatory virtue, and partly a tribute of gratitude for the stupendous service rendered them. It consisted of the "spoil," which, being the acquisition of individual valor, was not divided like the "prey," or livestock, each soldier retaining it in lieu of pay; it was offered by the "captains" alone, whose pious feelings were evinced by the dedication of the spoil which fell to their share. There were jewels to the amount of 16,750 shekels, equal to £87,869 16s. 5d. sterling.  <chapter eID="Num.31"/>

entries.352f91e2c72abdbe9956eceb1da015c290a0c72a: <div eID="gen6136" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6137" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6138" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6138" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6137" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6139" type="x-p"/> The command of the Lord to make war on the Midianites, <reference osisRef="Num.31.1">Num 31:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.2">Num 31:2</reference>. One thousand men are chosen out of each of the twelve tribes, and sent with Phinehas against the Midianites, <reference osisRef="Num.31.3-Num.31.6">Num 31:3-6</reference>. They slay all the males, <reference osisRef="Num.31.7">Num 31:7</reference>; their five kings and Balaam, <reference osisRef="Num.31.8">Num 31:8</reference>. They take all the women captives, with the flocks and goods, <reference osisRef="Num.31.9">Num 31:9</reference>; burn their cities, and bring away the spoil, <reference osisRef="Num.31.10">Num 31:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.11">Num 31:11</reference>. They bring the captives, etc., to Moses, who is wroth with the officers for sparing the women, who had formerly been the cause of their transgression and punishment, <reference osisRef="Num.31.12-Num.31.16">Num 31:12-16</reference>. He commands all the male children and all the grown up females to be slain, <reference osisRef="Num.31.17">Num 31:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.18">Num 31:18</reference>. How the soldiers were to purify themselves, <reference osisRef="Num.31.19">Num 31:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.20">Num 31:20</reference>; and the different articles taken in war, <reference osisRef="Num.31.21-Num.31.24">Num 31:21-24</reference>. They are commanded to take the sum of the prey, to divide it into two parts; one for the 12,000 warriors, and the other for the rest of the congregation, <reference osisRef="Num.31.25-Num.31.27">Num 31:25-27</reference>. One of 500, both of persons and cattle, of the share of the warriors, to be given to the Lord, <reference osisRef="Num.31.28">Num 31:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.29">Num 31:29</reference>; and one part of fifty, of the people's share, to be given to the Levites, <reference osisRef="Num.31.30">Num 31:30</reference>. The sum of the prey remaining after the above division; sheep 675,000, beeves 72,000, asses 61,000, young women 32,000, <reference osisRef="Num.31.31-Num.31.35">Num 31:31-35</reference>. How the soldiers' part was divided, <reference osisRef="Num.31.36-Num.31.40">Num 31:36-40</reference>. How the part belonging to the congregation was divided, <reference osisRef="Num.31.41-Num.31.47">Num 31:41-47</reference>. The officers report that they had not lost a man in this war, <reference osisRef="Num.31.48">Num 31:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.49">Num 31:49</reference>. They bring a voluntary oblation to God, of gold and ornaments, <reference osisRef="Num.31.50">Num 31:50</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.51">Num 31:51</reference>; the amount of which was 16,750 shekels, <reference osisRef="Num.31.52">Num 31:52</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.31.53">Num 31:53</reference>. Moses and Eleazar bring the gold into the tabernacle for a memorial, <reference osisRef="Num.31.54">Num 31:54</reference>.
entries.1304c2a527e54e219356b4f52f74136571d88b45: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen6139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6140" type="x-p"/> Gathered unto thy people - Where? Not in the grave surely. Moses was gathered with none of them, his burial-place no man ever knew. "But being gathered unto one's people means dying." It does imply dying, but it does not mean this only. The truth is, God considers all those who are dead to men in a state of conscious existence in another world. Therefore he calls himself the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob; now God is not the God of the dead, but of the living; because all Live to Him, whether dead to men or not. Moses therefore was to be gathered to his people - to enter into that republic of Israel which, having died in the faith, fear, and love of God, were now living in a state of conscious blessedness beyond the confines of the grave. See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.25.8">Gen 25:8</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Gen.49.33">Gen 49:33</reference> (note).
entries.76378b6ceee16588ede4eac49929eff7f3a34144: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen6140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6141" type="x-p"/> Avenge the Lord of Midian - It was God's quarrel, not their own, that they were now to take up. These people were idolaters; idolatry is an offense against God; the civil power has no authority to meddle with what belongs to Him, without especial directions, certified in the most unequivocal way. Private revenge, extension of territory, love of plunder, were to have no place in this business; the Lord is to be avenged; and through Him the children of Israel, (<reference osisRef="Num.31.2">Num 31:2</reference>), because their souls as well as their bodies had been well nigh ruined by their idolatry.
entries.dc91f04831039acc7d85bd96c68a5e097b4b5103: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen6141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6142" type="x-p"/> A thousand of every tribe - Twelve thousand men in the whole. And Phinehas, the son of Eleazar; some think he was made general in this expedition, but this is not likely. The ark and its contents must proceed to this battle, because the battle was the Lord's, and he dwelt between the cherubim over the ark; and Phinehas, who had before got a grant in the eternal priesthood, was chosen to accompany the ark in place of his father Eleazar, who was probably now too far advanced in years to undergo the fatigue. Who then was general? Joshua, without doubt, though not here mentioned, because the battle being the Lord's, he alone is to have the supreme direction, and all the glory. Besides, it was an extraordinary war, and not conducted on the common principle, for we do not find that peace was offered to the Midianites, and that they refused it; see <reference osisRef="Deu.20.10">Deu 20:10</reference>, etc. In such a case only hostilities could lawfully commence; but they were sinners against God; the cup of their iniquity was full, and God thought proper to destroy them. Though a leader there certainly was, and Joshua was probably that leader, yet because God, for the above reason, was considered as commander-in-chief, therefore no one else is mentioned; for it is evident that the sole business of Phinehas was to take care of the holy instruments and to blow with the trumpet.
entries.8eb949a7f12d422c7fb7f42506aaa1ed1190e4fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen6142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6143" type="x-p"/> Balaam - they slew with the sword - This man had probably committed what St. John calls the sin unto death - a sin which God punishes with temporal death, while at the same time he extends mercy to the soul. See the remarks at <reference osisRef="Num.24.25">Num 24:25</reference> (note).
entries.82648e26ef5ec6ad0dd299c8aa580b6be245b69d: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen6143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6144" type="x-p"/> Kill every male among the little ones - For this action I account simply on the principle that God, who is the author and supporter of life, has a right to dispose of it when and how he thinks proper; and the Judge of all the earth can do nothing but what is right. Of the women killed on this occasion it may be safely said, their lives were forfeited by their personal transgressions; and yet even in this case there can be little doubt that God showed mercy to their souls. The little ones were safely lodged; they were taken to heaven and saved from the evil to come.
entries.5cad291aea3677e6af8345bc59a006a0a2603279: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen6144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6145" type="x-p"/> The water of separation - The water in which the ashes of the red heifer were mingled; See <reference osisRef="Num.8.7">Num 8:7</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Num.19.2">Num 19:2</reference> (note), etc. Garments, whether of cloth or skins, were to be washed. Gold, silver, brass, iron, tin, and lead, to pass through the fire, probably to be melted down.
entries.1c1ca0bcaa12651786e73ebfc75d493d54ef1918: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen6145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6146" type="x-p"/> And levy a tribute unto the Lord - one soul of five hundred, etc. - The person to be employed in the Lord's service, under the Levites - the cattle either for sacrifice, or for the use of the Levites, <reference osisRef="Num.31.30">Num 31:30</reference>. Some monsters have supposed that one out of every five hundred of the captives was offered in sacrifice to the Lord! but this is abominable. When God chose to have the life of a man, he took it in the way of justice, as in the case of Midianites above, but never in the way of sacrifice.
entries.a8a14ae59b3c56c22129470dc886862d082c182c: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen6146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6147" type="x-p"/> The booty - It appears from the enumeration here that the Israelites, in this war against the Midianites, took 32,000 female prisoners, 61,000 asses, 72,000 beeves, 675,000 sheep and small cattle; besides the immense number of males who fell in battle, and the women and children who were slain by the Divine command, <reference osisRef="Num.31.17">Num 31:17</reference>. And it does not appear that in this expedition, a single man of Israel fell! This was naturally to be expected, because the battle was the Lord's, <reference osisRef="Num.31.49">Num 31:49</reference>. <div eID="gen6147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6148" type="x-p"/> As the booty was divided into two equal parts, <reference osisRef="Num.31.22">Num 31:22</reference>, one for the soldiers employed in the expedition, and the other for those who, being equally willing to be employed, were ordered to stay in the camp; so each of the parties in this booty was to give a certain proportion to the Lord. The soldiers to give to the Lord one out of every five hundred persons, beeves, asses, and sheep, <reference osisRef="Num.31.28">Num 31:28</reference>. The people, who by staying at home risked nothing, and had no fatigue, were to give one out of fifty of the above, <reference osisRef="Num.31.30">Num 31:30</reference>.
